questions.question: Do you use a gas burner purely out of necessity? I know you also use the wok on your induction.

hybrid.answer:
No, it isn't out of necessity. I use a portable butane burner because it works better for wok cooking, even when I had a full gas range at home [1]. The flame is concentrated and points up at the center, so more of the heat goes into the wok instead of up the sides [2]. A standard home burner spreads heat out evenly, which suits a flat skillet but not a wok [3].

I do cook on induction too. My new wok works on it, and you get good stir-frying out of it, but you can't get wok flavor [4]. A gas burner is essential for dishes that rely on wok hei, like dry-fried beef chow fun or fried rice [5].

If you have an induction or electric range, you can put a portable butane burner on top of it under your hood and vent the smoke [6]. I'd look for one around 12,500 BTU or more, and the most a butane canister can put out is around 15,000 BTU [7].

questions.question: How often do you oil your wooden cutting boards and utensils?

hybrid.answer:
I oil my cutting boards as needed, which works out to maybe a few times a year [1]. My wooden utensils probably get oiled less often than they should [2].

- **How I tell it's time:** A freshly oiled board gets a hydrophobic coating, so water beads up on it. As time goes on, water starts getting absorbed. If I see big stains developing, or I can't clean the board easily because water isn't beading, it's time to re-oil [3].
- **How I do it:** I use Howard Butcher Block conditioner [4] and rub it in with a paper towel or an oil rag [5].
- **When a board is beat up:** Once it's really beaten up or stained, I sand it with an orbital sander [5]. On one board I also trimmed the sides with a table saw, sanded everything, and chamfered the corners again to make it nearly new [5].

questions.question: Would you recommend a cleaver for breaking down the turkey frame? Any specific one?

hybrid.answer:
Yes, I'd recommend a cleaver for breaking down the turkey frame, and the one I'd point you to is the Shibazi Chinese cleaver [1]. It's a Chinese-style cleaver that you can get online for roughly 40 or 50 dollars, as best I remember [2]. I use it a lot because it stays sharp, the metal is pretty hard, and it's nice and heavy, so it gets through a turkey carcass pretty easily [2]. A cleaver is also useful alongside kitchen shears when spatchcocking. Use heavy-duty shears to get as far as you can on each side, then use the cleaver on any spot where a bone is too difficult for the shears [3].

questions.question: When should I salt my steak?

hybrid.answer:
I'd salt it well ahead of cooking: at least 45 minutes before, and ideally the night before, left uncovered in the fridge. [1][2]

**Why ahead of time works:** Salt first pulls moisture out of the steak, and then the brine breaks down some muscle proteins and gets reabsorbed. [3] Those broken-down proteins mean the steak holds onto moisture better, so it's juicier and more tender, and the seasoning goes deeper. [4][5]

**Overnight, uncovered:** Leaving it uncovered dries the surface and builds a pellicle, which makes it sear better. [6] Uncovered, the surface also becomes less hospitable to bacteria. [7] In my side-by-side, the steak salted overnight had a deeper mahogany crust than the unsalted one, which had a paler crust. [8]

**If you're short on time:** 45 minutes is about the minimum for the salt to work this way. [1] You can also sear right away, but don't cook it while there's lots of surface moisture, because that moisture robs the pan of heat. [9]

**Preference and limits:** An unsalted steak is still a good steak, and which texture you like is up to you. [10] I wouldn't go too far, though: a steak I salted for about 4 days ended up with a texture almost like ham. [11]

questions.question: Is the reverse sear still the best way to cook a steak?

hybrid.answer:
Yes. For a big, thick steak the reverse sear is still my favorite way to cook it, and it's the way I'd go with a steak that size [1]. I called it the best way for a home cook, since it gives an evenly cooked center, a crusty exterior and a wide margin for error [2].

**Why I like it**
- You start in a low oven and sear at the end, which gives even doneness from edge to center, instead of the bullseye gradient you get from searing first [3].
- The window of perfect doneness is much wider, probably 10 to 20 minutes before it starts to overcook in the oven, so it's easier to hit the doneness you want [4].
- The oven dries the surface, so you can sear better than you can a sous-vide steak, and it renders the fat a little better too. I actually prefer it to sous vide [5].
- You don't need to rest it afterward, because the temperature is already normalized through the steak [6].

**Where it applies**
- It works best on thick steaks. It's not really worth it for anything thinner than about an inch and a half [7].
- For a fatty cut like a ribeye I'd aim for medium-rare to medium. For leaner cuts like filet I'd aim for the rarer side [8].

questions.question: Which non-stick pan should I buy?

hybrid.answer:
I'd go for the Titanium Pro. It's the pan I use for virtually all my non-wok cooking [1]. I co-developed it with Our Place, so it's essentially my pan, and I know that makes it hard to take my word for it [2].

**Why I pick it over Teflon:** It's not as non-stick as Teflon, but it's better in most other respects [3]. Teflon has a very limited lifespan and a relatively low temperature range [4]. I also use metal utensils in the Titanium Pro, which you can't do with Teflon [5].

**Where Teflon still makes sense:** I mostly avoid non-stick these days, apart from a few specific uses, and I still use it for an omelet [6]. In my omelet test, the Titanium Pro slid out nearly as easily as the Teflon pan [7].

**Cast iron:** I'd use it if I wanted the best possible sear and was willing to put in more time and work [8].

questions.question: Is jarred pre-chopped garlic any good?

hybrid.answer:
No, I'd stay away from jarred pre-chopped garlic, whether it's packed in water or olive oil, because there's hardly any garlic flavor left in it [1]. Fresh garlic that you peel yourself is the best [2].

**Why:** Once garlic is cut open, its flavor starts to change and you can't change it back, so any pre-cut garlic tastes different from natural garlic flavor [3]. In my blind taste test, the two samples with a strong citric acid flavor tasted like citric acid water rather than garlic [4]. Citric acid is a preservative they use to control water activity and texture, and it completely changes the flavor [5]. I wouldn't recommend those for any raw use [5].

**If you do cook with it:** Any of these will sort of work for cooking, because cooking tames the sharper pungent flavors and evens out some of the differences [5]. Even so, there's not much aroma to them even before cooking [6].

**Better shortcuts:** Pre-peeled cloves are fine for most things, especially if you're cooking them, and garlic paste may be an acceptable substitute [1][7].

questions.question: Do you ever inject your turkey? And if so, any recommendations on what to use?

hybrid.answer:
I rarely inject my turkey. I've done it in the past, but it's not something I typically do [1]. When you inject, the liquid doesn't get inside the muscle fibers; it sloshes around and separates some of them, so the turkey comes out moist the way a sponge is wet, not the way a juicy piece of meat is [1].

If you do want to inject, here's what I'd recommend:

- **Well-seasoned stock:** This is the one good reason to inject. With salt in it, you're brining the turkey from the inside as well as the outside, which helps it retain more moisture when you cook and slice it [2].
- **Stock and brown butter:** I've done injections with a mixture of turkey stock and brown butter, and I think it can be delicious [2][3].
- **Herb-infused stock or herb butter:** You can simmer turkey stock with a lot of herbs, or melt an herb butter, combine it with the turkey stock and inject that [3].

questions.question: Why do you wash meat before stir-frying?

hybrid.answer:
I wash sliced meat before marinating because it makes the beef noticeably more tender, and it also helps the marinade work better. I never used to do this until I tested it side by side while working on my book, and it makes a huge difference [1].

- **Texture:** Squeezing and massaging the meat in plenty of cold water loosens up the texture of the muscle, so it comes out more tender. The difference is stark when you compare side by side [2].
- **Flavor:** The washing also squeezes out some of the excess juices. That leaves more room for the marinade to penetrate, so more flavor gets in [2].
- **Water chemistry:** A chef friend had the idea that in places with hard water, the slightly alkaline makeup of the water also affects the beef. I only mention that as his idea [2].

After washing, I squeeze the meat in a fine mesh strainer to get the excess water out so the marinade doesn't get watered down [3].

The washing step isn't in my older beef and broccoli video, but adding it would improve the texture of the beef there [4].

questions.question: Just wondering, what is the best way to clean the wok after each use? And should I use the heat & coat in oil technique after each use as well?

hybrid.answer:
Rinse it out, using soap if you need it, then put it back on the burner until it's completely dry, then rub in a very thin coat of oil. The heating isn't about seasoning; it's about getting the wok dry [1]. For stuck-on food, heat the wok, then scrub. A bamboo brush is the best tool for that [2].

**Heat and oil after each use?**
- I do it after cooking, but the oil step matters less if you cook in the wok every day or several times a day [3].
- It matters if you store the wok somewhere with moisture in the air, because an uncoated raw carbon steel wok can rust. With raw carbon steel, don't skip it [3].
- With a super nitrided wok it's not too much of an issue, because it isn't reactive the way carbon steel is [3].
- Keep the oil layer very thin: put some on, then wipe it out as if you'd put it there by accident. Too much can turn gummy over time [4].
- A nitrided wok doesn't need as much care about drying, but drying it on the burner still helps maintain the seasoning [5].

questions.question: A genuine question: if a wok doesn't build up layers of polymers like a cast iron, what does it mean for a wok to build up seasoning?

hybrid.answer:
For a wok, seasoning means converting raw carbon steel into black oxide, not stacking up polymer layers [1]. That is the initial seasoning, and it's what I mean when I talk about seasoning a wok [1].

- **Why polymers don't build up:** The bottom of a wok gets very hot while the edges stay cooler, so the metal expands unevenly and hard polymer layers have a tough time sticking [2]. Sauces, which are often acidic, also strip the seasoning when you deglaze [1].
- **What it looks like in use:** The first time you use raw carbon steel it turns black, and that black oxide layer can be considered seasoning [3]. After that, seasoning a wok is more of a per-use thing [3]. You shouldn't expect or aim for a thick polymer layer [3].

questions.question: Is there any advantage to salting hours ahead of time with this technique, or does the long time the steak spends hanging out in the oven make that moot? [reverse sear]

hybrid.answer:
Yes, I still salt ahead when I reverse sear. I season the steak heavily and let it sit about 45 minutes before it goes into the oven, which is about the minimum time for the salt to do its job [1]. The surface moisture matters less here because the steak goes into the oven first, but I still want that time for the salt to penetrate [2].

**What salting ahead gets you:**
- The salt breaks down some muscle proteins, so they tighten less when cooked and less moisture is squeezed out. You get a juicier steak and better, more penetrative seasoning [3].
- In a side-by-side with pan-seared tenderloin, the steak salted ahead ended up juicier and more tender [4].

**Going longer:** You can leave the steak uncovered in the fridge overnight instead of 45 minutes. The surface dries out and forms a pellicle, so it sears even better [5]. Forty-five minutes is enough, though [5].

I haven't directly tested whether the long oven time could stand in for salting ahead.

questions.question: So, Kenji, since you left Cook's Illustrated, they've started to advocate cold searing (starting in a cold pan and flipping every 2 minutes until done). What are your thoughts?

hybrid.answer: I haven't covered cold searing, or Cook's Illustrated's flip-every-two-minutes approach, in my videos yet. What I have said is that the reverse sear is still my favorite way to cook a big steak [1], and that I think it's the best way for a home cook to cook a steak because it gives an evenly cooked center and crusty exterior with a wide margin for error [2].
